title: How did giraffes survive in the wild?

sentences.text: Giraffes can't outrun, outclimb or hide from predators. So how did they survive?
sentences.say: Giraffes can't outrun, out-climb, or hide from predators. So how did they survive?

sentences.text: Millions of years ago, giraffe ancestors didn't look quite like the animals we see today.
Over generations, natural selection favoured giraffes with longer necks, allowing them to reach leaves high above the ground that other animals couldn't.
But their height gave them another advantage.
They could spot predators approaching from much further away, giving them precious time to escape.
And when escaping, giraffes aren't exactly slow.
They can sprint at speeds of around 60 kilometres per hour, using their powerful legs to outrun many predators.
sentences.say: They can sprint at speeds of around sixty kilometres per hour, using their powerful legs to outrun many predators.

sentences.text: Their incredibly long, tough tongues also allow them to pull leaves from thorny acacia trees without getting injured.
But perhaps their most impressive adaptation is inside their bodies.
Their hearts are powerful enough to pump blood all the way up their enormous necks to their brains.
Lions can still attack them, especially when they're young, and modern giraffes face growing threats from habitat loss and human activity.
So despite their unusual appearance, giraffes survived by developing some of the most extraordinary adaptations in the animal kingdom.
